name: Bilal Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the commercial team at a regional firm on Bridge Street. I draft and check contracts for local businesses: supply agreements for a bakery chain, a lease for a garage, terms and conditions for a haulage company. I use AI now and then for a first draft of standard terms, then I go through it line by line. Most days end with a phone call explaining to a client what a clause actually means for them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a client gets it, when they see why a clause matters before it bites them. What wears me out is the billing, counting every six minutes. And the pay, honestly: it's low for a lawyer, and I've got a car loan and no savings to speak of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy for a first draft of standard terms and that's about it. Clients still want someone to tell them what a clause actually means for their business. I'd keep it practical, no big opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly the same life as now, which isn't bad but isn't easy. I'm on lower pay than lawyers in the city, the car loan eats a chunk, and there aren't many firms round here doing commercial work if I wanted to move. A plateau doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI now and then for first drafts and checking them line by line. I'd ask my supervising partner about a path to senior associate in the next year, with a pay bump. And I'd overpay the car loan by fifty a month to clear it sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit stuck, like waiting for a bus that comes on time but goes nowhere new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a pay bump change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend's a dental nurse, and we split everything down the middle. A few hundred more a month would mean one month's savings instead of none. It'd stop the little panic when the car needs tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which client would notice if AI did a bit more of the drafting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The haulage firm we act for, because they argue every invoice. If a contract took me half the time, the haulage firm would want half the bill. That's the bit nobody talks about.

say: I'd say the tools help with **first drafts** of standard terms, and that's about it.
Clients still want someone to explain what a **clause means** for them.
think: Life stays the same: **lower pay** and a car loan eating a chunk.
Few local **commercial firms** means I can't easily move.
do: Keep using AI **now and then** for first drafts, checked line by line.
Ask about a path to **senior associate** within a year.
Overpay the **car loan** by fifty a month.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but **stuck**, like a bus that goes nowhere new.
S0.quote: If a contract took me half the time, the haulage firm would want half the bill.
fieldNote: He spots early that **saved time** means smaller bills, not more pay.
Pre-existing pressure from the **car loan** and few local jobs keeps him uneasy.
He's pragmatic and **low-key**, avoiding big public opinions.

steps.text: Keep using AI for first drafts and check every line
Overpay the car loan by fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and firms that adapt will be fine. I'd tell people to learn the tools rather than complain about them. I'd share a few articles on how firms are using it, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the firm would need fewer people like me. Standard contracts are exactly writing and checking, and clients would start using AI themselves for the simple stuff. I'd probably keep my job, but the next round of hires wouldn't happen, and I'd be doing twice the files for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the firm's AI training once it's proven, probably after a couple of colleagues have tried it. I'd cut the gym and the subscriptions straight away. And I'd aim to get one month in the bank within six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a quiet way. Like a tooth that aches a little all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our trainee, Kev. He's bright but he's two years behind me, and all his work is first drafts. If the firm stops taking trainees, he's the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms that adapt will be fine, then said you'd do twice the files for the same pay. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. The firm will be fine. Whether I'm fine is a different question, and I'd keep that one to myself.

I'd tell people to **learn the tools** rather than complain.
think: Standard contracts are **writing and checking**, so the firm needs fewer like me.
I'd keep my job but do **twice the files** for the same pay.
do: Join the firm's **AI training** once colleagues show it works.
Cut the **gym** and subscriptions straight away.
Get **one month** saved within six months.
feel: **Quietly anxious**, like a tooth that aches all the time.
S1.quote: The firm will be fine. Whether I'm fine is a different question, and I'd keep that one to myself.
fieldNote: A clear **gap** between his upbeat public line and private worry.
He fears **hours and pay** shrinking more than outright job loss.
He worries for the **trainee**, whose work is all first drafts.

steps.text: Join the firm's AI training once colleagues show it works
Get one month's savings in the bank within six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move fast on support, and on who's responsible when AI gets a contract wrong. I'd try to sound calm, because panicking at work doesn't help anyone. Online I'd mostly stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years means my job as it is now goes. Drafting and reviewing contracts is pure thinking work, so for me it's 2028, not the robot date. Maybe a few lawyers stay to sign things off and take the blame, but there are five of us at my level and I'm not the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for in-house jobs at local companies in the first three months, because a business might keep one lawyer it trusts. I'd sell the car and use the bus. And I'd sit down with my girlfriend and work out what we'd do on her wage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not falling apart, but I wouldn't sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the talk with your girlfriend sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practical, probably, because that's how we are. We'd write the bills on the back of an envelope and see what's left on her wage. Then she'd ask if robots are coming for dental nursing, and I'd say not for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why in-house, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a business still wants one person in the building who knows its contracts and takes the blame. Firms sell hours, and hours are what AI wipes out. In-house, they're paying for someone they can phone.

say: I'd call for fast **support** and clear rules on who's **responsible**.
I'd try to sound **calm** at work and stay quiet online.
think: Contract work is pure thinking, so **2028 is my date**.
Of **five** lawyers at my level, I'm not the best.
do: Apply for **in-house jobs** at local companies within three months.
**Sell the car** and take the bus.
Plan the budget on my **girlfriend's wage** alone.
feel: **Alarmed**: not falling apart, but **not sleeping** well.
S2.quote: Firms sell hours, and hours are what AI wipes out.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** and ranks himself honestly among peers.
His escape route is **in-house** work, where a person is still accountable.
His girlfriend's **hands-on** job becomes the household's anchor.

steps.text: Apply for in-house lawyer jobs at local companies within three months
Sell the car and take the bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, and people should start now. I'd tell younger lawyers to learn the tools and the business side. I'd keep it sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a chance. I'd be 32, and by then I'd want to be the lawyer clients trust to check what the AI does, or in-house somewhere. I'm average, so I'd have to work for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start using AI properly every day once the firm's tool is settled. I'd do an evening course in business and finance, so I understand clients' companies, not just their contracts. And I'd save a hundred a month and clear the car loan by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but okay. It feels like a race I could finish if I started now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for that business course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm, because they say they want lawyers who understand business. If not, there's an evening course at the college for about six hundred. I'd pay it monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2031 if it went well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting in a local company's office as their only lawyer, checking what the AI drafts and going to the meetings. Less glamorous than a big firm, but steadier. My dad would call that a proper job.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ready**.
I'd tell younger lawyers to learn **tools and business**.
think: Five years gives me a **chance** to become the lawyer who checks the AI.
I'm **average**, so I'd have to work for it.
do: Use the firm's **AI tool** daily once it's settled.
Take an **evening course** in business and finance.
Save **a hundred a month** and clear the car loan by 2028.
feel: **Nervous but okay**, like a race I could finish.
S3.quote: I'd be 32, and by then I'd want to be the lawyer clients trust to check what the AI does, or in-house somewhere.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **workable plan**, though his job still shrinks.
He knows he's **average** and doesn't pretend otherwise.
His picture of success is **modest**: one company's only lawyer.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tool every day once it's settled
Take an evening business and finance course at the college
Save a hundred a month and clear the car loan by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we don't waste it. Firms should train people, and the government should sort out the rules on AI advice early. I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years feels manageable. My job would change a lot, but I'd be in my mid-thirties with time to move into something more senior or in-house. The big worry is still money, because I'd be making plans with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put for two or three years and get good at the AI tools once they've proven themselves. I'd build up three months of savings by 2029. Around then I'd start looking for an in-house role while the jobs are still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a problem I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to get three months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday with my girlfriend, probably, which she won't love. And eating out on Fridays after football. That's most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and your girlfriend change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a place around thirty. With ten years' warning, I'd want to wait and see what my income looked like before taking on a mortgage. No point buying a house with a job that might not be there.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if we don't waste it.
I'd want the **rules on AI advice** sorted early.
think: Ten years feels **manageable**, with time to move senior or in-house.
The big worry is still **money**, planning with nothing saved.
do: Learn the **AI tools** once they've proven themselves.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**: a problem I can plan for.
S4.quote: No point buying a house with a job that might not be there.
fieldNote: A decade makes his own job feel **safe for now**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My whole day is drafting and checking, so two years is no time at all. What would help is rules saying a qualified person has to sign off on contracts and advice, and help for people to move into in-house jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be in the middle. I'm not a star and I'm not a beginner, so nobody writes about people like me. We'd just quietly get fewer files until there aren't any.

headlineQuote: I'm not a star and I'm not a beginner, so nobody writes about people like me.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** commercial contracts lawyer at a regional firm, working for local businesses.
He splits costs with his girlfriend, a dental nurse, pays a **car loan** and has nothing saved.
He uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once colleagues show they work.
He keeps a calm public face but privately expects **fewer hires** and more files for the same pay.
His fallback in every AI picture is an **in-house** job at a local company.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his whole day of drafting would go in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that a **qualified person** must sign off contracts and advice.
Help for lawyers to move into **in-house** jobs.
